content: When conducting screening activities related to Marburg disease where maintaining a distance of at least 1 meter is not feasible, the use of a face shield combined with a medical mask is recommended as an intervention. This is compared to the use of a face shield alone. Initial searches and screenings for key questions regarding the use of face shields versus masks, and gowns versus coveralls, were conducted together due to the thematic similarity of these questions under the broader topic of personal protective equipment (PPE) use for health and care workers during screening and triage activities. A total of 393 studies were screened using the CAL tool software, and 86 studies were selected for full-text screening. Two systematic reviews of potential interest were identified, but none of the 86 reviewed studies or the studies included in the systematic reviews met the eligibility criteria for the key questions. Key findings from contextual data extraction include the following: Basic PPE ensembles (gloves, surgical masks, and visors) were less effective than more protective PPE ensembles, such as the gown model or coverall model. PPE with more protective gear provided slightly better protection against contamination in simulation studies but was reported to be less comfortable for health and care workers. For example: Gowns resulted in less contamination compared to aprons. Using two pairs of gloves led to less contamination than using only one pair. The peak of contagiousness for Marburg and Ebola viruses occurs around the time of death. However, patients presenting to healthcare facilities for screening and triage often do so after the onset of symptoms or are already contagious at the time of screening and triage. The systematic review did not identify any evidence regarding the effects of wearing a face shield alone versus a face shield combined with a medical mask on outcomes such as infection with Ebola or Marburg viruses, PPE breaches (e.g., touching the face), or compliance related to heat, humidity, and comfort. No studies were found that addressed these outcomes. Regarding the use of gowns versus coveralls, no evidence was identified to determine the effects of wearing a coverall compared to a gown on infection rates with Ebola or Marburg viruses, PPE breaches, or compliance related to heat, comfort, human factors, and health worker confidence. Similarly, no studies were found that examined these outcomes. A total of 273 studies were screened for the question of using two pairs of gloves versus one pair during screening and triage activities where maintaining a 1-meter distance is not possible. Of these, 74 studies were included for full-text screening. However, no studies met the eligibility criteria. Most studies were excluded because the health workers in the studies were not performing screening or triage activities, or there was no relevant intervention or comparator. From the systematic review by Verbeek et al., one additional article was identified that discussed the comparative effect of wearing double gloves versus single gloves on Ebola contamination rates during PPE donning and doffing activities. However, this study did not meet the eligibility criteria.
